sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Kṣitigarbha** (*ksitigarbha*) — Earth Womb, Savior of Hell Beings · The Earth-Womb, Vow to Empty the Hells — is the bodhisattva who made the most extreme vow in Buddhism: not to attain Buddhahood until every hell is empty.[^1]

His name joins *kṣiti*, ‘earth’, with *garbha*, ‘womb, embryo, inner chamber’ — ‘Earth-Womb’, or as the Chinese render him, Dìzàng 地藏, ‘Earth-Store’: the bodhisattva in whom the earth's patience and a mother's compassion are one. Monk-robed, shaven-headed, carrying the six-ringed staff whose jingle warns the small creatures and the cintāmaṇi jewel that lights the darkest roads, he is the patron of travellers, children, and the dead — above all of the beings in the hells, whom he visits age after age rather than rest.[^2] In China he is Dìzàng, lord of Mount Jiuhua; in Japan, [[jizo|Jizō]], the most beloved figure of the roadside and the graveyard.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Kṣitigarbha** and serves its temple at [kṣitigarbha.com](https://xn--kitigarbha-wy2e.com). The restoration keeps the retroflex ṣ of the initial cluster kṣ; the plain ASCII *ksitigarbha* is a modern convenience of the early domain-name system, not an attested ancient spelling.[^3]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Kṣitigarbha’.
Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva: Dizang in Medieval China (Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. kṣiti, garbha.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Sanskrit as **क्षितिगर्भ** (IAST *kṣitigarbha*): a tatpuruṣa compound of *kṣiti*, ‘earth’ (from √*kṣi*, ‘to dwell, abide’ — the earth as the dwelling-place), and *garbha*, ‘womb, embryo, innermost chamber’ — ‘Earth-Womb’, ‘the womb of the earth’.[^1] The image is generative patience: the earth holds every seed in darkness and asks nothing. The Chinese translation Dìzàng 地藏, ‘Earth-Store’, and the Japanese Jizō 地蔵 carry the same metaphor, and Tibetan renders the name Sā'i snying po (Sayi Nyingpo), ‘Essence of the Earth’.

The ASCII form *ksitigarbha* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling, and it opens the name with the unpronounceable-looking ASCII cluster *ks-* that the retroflex ṣ resolves. The Unicode restoration **Kṣitigarbha** recovers the retroflex directly in the address bar. Because the restoration preserves a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses, the name is classified Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **k** → **K** — Same, capitalized
- **s** → **ṣ** — Retroflex ṣ (the kṣ cluster)
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **b** → **b** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The project holds the domain **kṣitigarbha.com** (xn--kitigarbha-wy2e.com) as the canonical home of this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. kṣiti, garbha, kṣitigarbha.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Grammar and Dictionary, vol. 2 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Kṣitigarbha.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/kʂi.ti.ˈɡəɾ.bʱə/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Kṣi-** — The cluster [kʂ], voiceless velar plus retroflex sibilant, with short [i]: ‘earth’
- **-ti-** — Voiceless dental [t] with short [i]
- **-gar-** — Voiced velar [g] with short [ə] and tapped [r]; the stressed syllable of *garbha*, ‘womb’
- **-bha** — Voiced aspirated bilabial [bʱ] with short [ə]; one breathy sound, not b + h

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘kshi-tih-GUR-bhuh’ — the opening cluster like the *ksh* in ‘backseat’ said quickly.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — क्षितिगर्भ (kṣitigarbha), ‘Earth-Womb’
- **Chinese** — 地藏 (Dìzàng), ‘Earth-Store’
- **Japanese** — Jizō; **Korean** — Jijang
- **Tibetan** — Sā'i snying po (Sayi Nyingpo), ‘Essence of the Earth’

Kṣitigarbha is Tier 1 because the retroflex ṣ is a distinctive letter ASCII cannot carry; the ‘ks’ of the fallback is an accident of transliteration.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. kṣitigarbha.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **क्षितिगर्भ** — Brahmic abugida, attested Buddhist Sanskrit, in the sūtra manuscripts of India and Nepal; the script is written left-to-right.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Kṣitigarbha* (IAST), giving the normalized reading /kʂi.ti.ˈɡəɾ.bʱə/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha is written क्षितिगर्भ in Devanagari: क्षि (kṣi) + ति (ti) + गर्भ (garbha); the conjunct क्ष — the same ligature that opens [[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]]'s name — writes the cluster kṣ.
- The compound is kṣiti (‘earth’, from √kṣi, ‘to dwell’) + garbha (‘womb, embryo, inner chamber’): ‘Earth-Womb’.
- IAST writes the retroflex sibilant as ṣ, distinguishing it from palatal ś and dental s.
- The Unicode restoration Kṣitigarbha is registrable in .com; the Devanagari form is not supported in the .com IDN table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. kṣiti, garbha.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Kṣitigarbha.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Kṣitigarbha** is the bodhisattva of the lowest places: the one who goes down, age after age, where no other saviour will look.[^1]

### The Hells

His vow — ‘until the hells are empty, I shall not become a Buddha’ — makes him the patron of the damned themselves: the beings furthest from rescue are his congregation.

### The Dead and the Dying

He shepherds souls through the intermediate state and the courts of the underworld, the guide of the recently dead.

### Children and Travellers

As Jizō in Japan he guards children — above all those who died young — and travellers on every road: his statues stand where the path is dark.[^2]

### The Earth's Patience

His name is his method: like the earth, he holds every being in the dark until it ripens; the womb, not the throne, is his emblem.

sources.citation: Kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra (Sūtra of the Past Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva, T. 412).
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life: Abortion and Buddhism in Japan (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1992), on mizuko Jizō.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography of Kṣitigarbha is deliberately plain — a monk, not a prince — and every item is a tool of rescue:[^1]

- **The khakkhara staff** — The six-ringed mendicant's staff whose rings jingle to warn living creatures from the path; in the underworld tradition its sound opens the gates of the hells
- **The cintāmaṇi jewel** — The wish-fulfilling gem held in the left hand, glowing with the light that illumines the darkest ways: the lantern of the six realms
- **The monk's robe and shaven head** — The only great bodhisattva figured as a simple bhikṣu: rescue dresses for work, not for court
- **The patched robes of Jizō** — In Japan his statues wear red bibs and caps offered by grieving parents: the only iconography in Buddhism knitted by the bereaved[^2]
- **Mount Jiuhua** — His earthly seat in Anhui, one of the four sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism, where his body is enshrined

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1914).
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life (Princeton University Press, 1992).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Kṣitigarbha's mythology is a cycle of vows and descents, preserved above all in the Sūtra of the Past Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva (Taishō 412), the most beloved scripture of East Asian devotion to the dead.[^1]

### The Brahmin Daughter

In a past age, the sūtra tells, he was a Brahmin girl whose mother died scoffing at the Three Jewels and fell into the Avīci hell. The daughter sold everything, made offerings before the Buddha of that era, and by the merit and by her own piercing meditation saw her mother raised to a better rebirth — and then, before the Buddha's image, she made the vow that defines him: that through measureless aeons she would work for the deliverance of all beings in the evil destinies, everywhere, without exception. The saviour of the hells began as a daughter who would not accept her mother's damnation.[^2]

### The Two Kings

The sūtra's second vow-story makes the same point from the other side: two kings of a former age, friends, both resolved to save their people. One vowed to attain Buddhahood quickly, the better to help; the other vowed to save every suffering being first and only then awaken. The first is long since a Buddha; the second is Kṣitigarbha still — the bodhisattva who chose to be last.[^2]

### The Lord of the Underworld (China)

In medieval China, Dìzàng's cult fused with the indigenous courts of the dead: the apocryphal Scripture on the Ten Kings made him overseer of the ten magistrates who judge the dead, the compassionate superior of the entire infernal bureaucracy. Zhiru Ng's study documents how this foreign bodhisattva became, in a few centuries, the Chinese dead's foremost advocate.[^3]

### The Korean Incarnation (Mount Jiuhua)

The tradition's boldest claim is biographical: the Silla prince-monk Jin Qiaojue (Kim Gyo-gak, d. 794), who practised for seventy-five years at Mount Jiuhua in Anhui, was revered after death as Dìzàng's emanation — his body, enshrined and undecayed, made the mountain the bodhisattva's earthly residence, one of the four sacred peaks of Chinese Buddhism.[^3]

sources.citation: Kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra (T. 412).
Kṣitigarbha Sūtra, ch. 1 (the Brahmin daughter; the two kings).
Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva: Dizang in Medieval China (University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
No bodhisattva was more thoroughly re-made by East Asia. In China the Sanskrit Earth-Womb became Dìzàng, absorbed the underworld bureaucracy of the Ten Kings, and took up residence at Mount Jiuhua through the Korean monk Jin Qiaojue — an Indian bodhisattva incarnated, by pious consensus, as a Korean prince on a Chinese mountain.[^1] In Japan he became [[jizo|Jizō]], and the transformation completed itself: the saviour of hells became the small stone figure at every crossroads, guardian of children and travellers, and — in the modern mizuko rites — the comforter of aborted and stillborn children, the most intimate cult in Japanese Buddhism.[^2]

Korea keeps him as Jijang, second in devotion only to Avalokiteśvara; Tibet honours Sayi Nyingpo among the eight great bodhisattvas. His nearest kin in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index are [[guanyin|Guānyīn]] (the other face of East Asian compassion) and [[mara|Māra]] (the lord of death whose kingdom he has sworn to empty).

sources.citation: Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva (University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life (Princeton University Press, 1992).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Kṣitigarbha's legacy is measured in the smallest monuments of Asia: the roadside Jizō of Japan — bibs red, caps knitted, toys piled at the base — tended by strangers for other strangers' children; the funeral liturgies of China, where the Earth Store Sūtra is still the standard scripture for the dead; and the pilgrimage of Mount Jiuhua, where his embodied presence has drawn the grieving and the faithful for twelve centuries.[^1]

His vow has become the tradition's own conscience. ‘Until the hells are empty’ is quoted wherever Buddhism talks about the bottom line of compassion — the refusal to be saved first — and the mizuko rites documented by LaFleur have made his name, in our own century, part of the hardest conversations in Japanese society.[^2]

sources.citation: Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva (University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life (Princeton University Press, 1992).

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
The monumental record begins at **Dunhuang**: the Mogao cave shrines preserve numerous Tang and Five Dynasties paintings of Dìzàng — alone with his staff, or enthroned above the Ten Kings of the underworld — the documentary archive of his rise in medieval China.[^1] **Mount Jiuhua** in Anhui is the living monument: its monasteries have kept the cult since the eighth century, and the Roushen (‘Flesh Body’) Hall enshrines the preserved body of Jin Qiaojue, the Silla monk venerated as Dìzàng's embodiment — a case unique in Buddhism of a bodhisattva with a postal address and a body.

In Japan the record is deliberately modest and therefore immense: uncounted stone Jizō at crossroads, mountain passes, and temple grounds, many centuries old, the largest body of vernacular religious sculpture in the country — archaeology of compassion, unsigned.[^2]

sources.citation: Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva (University of Hawai'i Press, 2007), on the Dunhuang material and Jiuhuashan.
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life (Princeton University Press, 1992).

sections.label: Pāli Canon
sections.body:
**Kṣitigarbha is absent from the Pāli Canon.** The Tipiṭaka knows no bodhisattva of this name; its concern for the dead runs through the doctrines of kamma, rebirth, and the dedication of merit, not through a celestial rescuer of the hells. The cult of the Earth-Womb belongs to the Mahāyāna sūtra literature and its Chinese and Japanese developments.[^1]

The canon's own practice of merit-transference — the Tirokudda Sutta's teaching that gifts given in the dead's name reach the departed — is the early stratum on which the whole Dìzàng cult would later build its economy of rescue.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Kṣitigarbha’.
Khuddakapāṭha 7 (Tirokudda Sutta), on merit for the dead.

sections.label: Mahāyāna Sūtras
sections.body:
Three sūtras constitute his canon. The **Sūtra of the Past Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva** (Taishō 412, the ‘Kṣitigarbha Sūtra’, translated into Chinese in the late seventh century and ascribed to Śikṣānanda) is the devotional charter: the Brahmin daughter's rescue of her mother, the two kings' vows, the description of the hells, and the great vow itself — the most recited funeral scripture of East Asia.[^1]

The **Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha Sūtra** (‘Ten Wheels’, T. 410–411) preserves the older Indic stratum: Kṣitigarbha as the bodhisattva of the ‘sage of the ten powers' retinue, praised by the Buddha above other bodhisattvas for his work among beings in the evil destinies. The Chinese apocryphal literature — above all the **Scripture on the Ten Kings** — then built his underworld chancellery, the documentable growth of a saviour from sūtra to bureaucracy.[^2]

sources.citation: Kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra (T. 412); Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha Sūtra (T. 410–411).
Teiser, Stephen F., The Scripture on the Ten Kings (University of Hawai'i Press, 1994).

sections.label: Commentarial Tradition
sections.body:
India left little śāstra literature on Kṣitigarbha; his interpretation happened in China. The medieval exegetes read the Ten Wheels and the Past Vows into a complete theology of the underworld — hell as transformable, judgment as merciful, the bodhisattva as the bureaucracy's conscience — and the ritual manuals of the Ten Kings made that theology a working funeral liturgy.[^1]

In Japan the commentarial tradition is largely vernacular: the Jizō-and-children narratives, the sai-no-kawara legend of the children piling stones by the river of death whom Jizō gathers into his sleeves, and the modern mizuko liturgies documented by LaFleur constitute a folk exegesis as authoritative in practice as any śāstra. Mount Jiuhua's own chronicles, meanwhile, read the mountain's whole history as the bodhisattva's biography.[^2]

sources.citation: Teiser, Stephen F., The Scripture on the Ten Kings (University of Hawai'i Press, 1994); Ng, Zhiru, The Making of a Savior Bodhisattva (University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).
LaFleur, William R., Liquid Life (Princeton University Press, 1992).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every religion has a doctrine of the last place in line. Kṣitigarbha is Buddhism's: the bodhisattva who looked at the queue for salvation and went to the back of it, permanently. The vow is, by design, unfulfillable — the hells refill as fast as they empty — and that is precisely its meaning: compassion is not a project with a completion date.

He is also the tradition's answer to an unbearable question: what about the ones no one wants — the worst, the forgotten, the stillborn, the damned? His answer is a shaven head and a jingling staff at the bottom of everything: them first. The Earth-Womb holds what the world discards, the way the earth holds every seed in the dark and calls it not waste but winter.

sources.citation: Kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra (T. 412).
